Audit

How Slopographic works

The apps run in your browser. This page lists the browser features they use, every network request they can make, and what is kept on your device, so you can check each claim yourself. Every statement here was checked against the source code in the public repository.

The short version

  • Your files stay on your device. The apps have no server that receives them, and no code uploads a file you open or save.
  • Files you choose on disk are read and written through the browser's File System Access API, in the folders you pick. See the browser APIs.
  • Data is kept in the browser's own storage on this device (IndexedDB and localStorage). See what is stored.
  • Some requests leave the site, but only in the cases listed in every outbound request: a download you confirm, a cloud backup you connect, the exchange rates you turn on, analytics or ads you accept.
  • The homepage loads Google Analytics code on each visit with analytics set to denied. Other pages load it only after you accept analytics. Ads load only after you accept ads.

In plain words

Where do my files go?

Nowhere. When you open a photo, a PDF or a spreadsheet, the app reads it inside this browser tab. There is no upload step and no Slopographic server that could receive it. What you save goes to your own disk, or to this browser's storage on this device.

Why does an app sometimes download something?

Some features need a large file that most people never use: an AI model (to remove a background, read text or transcribe speech), the video engine (to convert a video), or a font for another writing system. These are fetched only when you use the feature, after the app tells you what it is and how big it is, and they are kept in the browser so it happens once. Your own files are never part of that request.

Does it work offline?

Yes, after the first visit. The site's own files are kept by the browser, so the apps open and work without a connection. Only a download you have not made yet (a model or a font) needs the network.

Do I need to install anything?

No. Just open an app in the browser on your phone, tablet or computer and start. It keeps working without internet after your first visit. Want an icon on your home screen? On iPhone or iPad, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. On Android, open the browser menu and tap Add to Home screen. On a computer, click the install icon in the address bar. You do not need the App Store or Google Play, and your files stay on your device.

Can an AI agent use the apps?

In a browser that supports WebMCP, yes: an assistant in the browser, or an agent on your computer connected through a browser extension, can run an app's commands, File convert conversions and workflows, and open, save or download files. It refers to your files by ids; the work runs in this tab and the apps upload nothing, though the agent sees what the tools report back. Anything that deletes or replaces your work asks you first. WebMCP is an early draft: Chrome has it in a trial (versions 149 to 156) and behind a flag, Edge behind a flag, and Firefox and Safari not yet. Turn it off in Settings, or in Help, AI agents.

Can I check this myself?

Yes. The source code is public, and the sections below list every browser feature the apps use and every request they can make, with the file that makes it. You can also open your browser's developer tools, go to the Network tab and watch: opening and saving your files sends nothing.

Use Slopographic from Claude Code and other AI apps

Coming soon: an AI app on your computer, such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code or Claude Desktop, can use the Slopographic app open in your browser: its real commands, conversions and workflows, with your files going in and results coming out as files on your computer. It runs through the Slopographic MCP server, a small program the AI app starts on your computer. It needs no account and no install beyond the AI app itself.

  1. Claude Code: type /plugin marketplace add slopographic/claude-plugin, then /plugin install slopographic@slopographic. Do this once.
  2. Type /slopographic:slop-connect (add an app name, such as photoslop, if you like). Claude Code opens Slopographic in your browser and shows a short code.
  3. Chrome asks once whether this site may use apps and services on this device. Choose Allow: that is how the page reaches Claude Code on your computer. The page talks only to your own computer (127.0.0.1), not to your network.
  4. Type the code in the page. The page then shows “Claude Code is connected · Disconnect” in the corner. Press Disconnect, or close the tab, to end it.

Each tab is paired on its own, and the code works once. Nothing else on your computer can use the page without it. Actions that delete or replace your work still ask you in the page, as in the AI panel. Any Slopographic page can connect from the command palette: Ctrl+K (⌘K on a Mac), then “Connect an AI app…”.

The setup for other AI apps (Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Claude Desktop) appears here when scripts run.

ChatGPT chats can only reach servers on the internet, so they cannot use this local server yet. Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app can.

Cookies: the site's code never writes a cookie (the repository has no document.cookie call). Your consent choice is in localStorage, not a cookie. Google's analytics and ads scripts may set their own cookies when they run. Section Cookies and analytics says when they run.

Two things that look like network use but are not: tools/vendor-codemirror.mjs fetches packages from cdn.jsdelivr.net when a developer runs it by hand to refresh the vendored code. Cookies and analytics

  • Stored by the site's code: a consent choice in localStorage (slop-consent), with analytics, ads and rates set to off until you choose. Storage can be cleared in the browser at any time.
  • Not stored by the site's code: no cookie and no account. The repository never writes a cookie.
  • Google Analytics: on the homepage, the tag is loaded with analytics_storage set to denied. It is switched on only when you accept analytics. On other pages it loads only after you accept.
  • Google's own scripts may set cookies of their own when they run. That is decided by Google, not by Slopographic code. The audit steps below show what the browser actually stores.
  • Ads: AdSense loads only after you accept ads. Refusing the ads leaves the ad slots empty.

Working offline

After one visit, the site's own files are kept in Cache Storage by the service worker (service-worker.js, with its file list in sw-precache.js). Pages are checked over the network first, then taken from the cache, and then the offline page is shown. Your files are not in the service worker cache: they are in the folder you picked, or in IndexedDB. The apps keep working with the network off. Downloads (the models and font packs listed above) need the network the first time.

How to check it yourself

  1. Network tab, with the page loaded. Open the app, press F12 (or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac), and open the Network tab. Tick "Preserve log", then reload. Read the Domain column. On a plain visit, you should see only slopographic.com, plus Google's analytics domains on the homepage.
  2. Network tab, offline. In the Network tab, open the throttling menu and choose Offline. Reload, then open a file, edit it and save it. The app should work. Anything that needs a download says so.
  3. Application tab, storage. In Chrome or Edge, open the Application tab. Under Storage, see Local storage, Session storage, IndexedDB, Cookies, Cache Storage and Service workers. Compare what you see with the tables on this page.
  4. Accept or refuse, then compare. Refuse analytics and ads in the consent strip, reload, and check the Network tab again. Then accept them, and see which requests appear.
  5. Read the source. The code is public in the slopographic repository on GitHub. Search it for fetch(, indexedDB.open, localStorage or showDirectoryPicker to confirm any row on this page. The consent code is in shared/consent/, cloud sync in shared/sync/, and the download lists in shared/library/ and aitools/.

Local folders (the File System Access API) need Chrome or Edge. Firefox and Safari do not offer them, and the apps say so where it applies.
